lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Good morning and welcome to The Daily Grind. I'm Milo, and my mug today is large enough to qualify as a zoning issue.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: And I'm Riley. It is Saturday, May 09, and the coffee world has business deals, science, competition prep, and a little supply-chain anxiety in the hopper.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: So, a normal week in coffee: beautiful aromatics on top, macroeconomics underneath, and someone somewhere adjusting grind size with the intensity of a safecracker.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: Exactly. Let's start with Daily Coffee News' May eighth weekly roundup, because it had a lot packed into one cup.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Headline one: Dean's Beans Organic Coffee Company in Orange, Massachusetts was named Rural Business of the Year for Massachusetts by the U.S. Small Business Administration.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: And that is not just a plaque moment. The SBA cited the worker-owned roaster's ethical sourcing practices, and Dean's Beans also posted a B Corp recertification score of 168.5.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: For context, the B Corp certification threshold is 80. So 168.5 is not squeaking by; that is showing up with a thermos and extra pencils.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: It is a reminder that small and midsize roasters can still lead on values, sourcing, and governance while competing in an industry that keeps consolidating.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: The same roundup also noted Fairtrade International's 2026 to 2028 strategy, centered on sustainable livelihoods, resilient supply chains, and getting more people committed to fair trade.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: Which sounds broad, but in this market, broad is necessary. Producers are dealing with climate volatility, input costs, currency pressure, and buyers who want both traceability and affordability.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Then there was Lavazza launching a professional-focused regenerative coffee sourced under the Rainforest Alliance's new Regenerative Agriculture Standard.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: I like that regenerative is moving into B2B coffee, not just retail storytelling. Offices, hotels, restaurants, and cafes can move real volume if the sourcing is credible.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: The cynical barista in me asks whether every bag will soon say regenerative, climate-smart, moon-blessed, and emotionally available.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: Fair. The labels need proof behind them. But if standards improve soil health, biodiversity, and farmer resilience, I will allow one tastefully designed badge.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Daily Coffee News also reported Starbucks announcing a three-year initiative with the Integrated Tribal Development Foundation in northern Thailand.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: That project focuses on farming and post-harvest practices to improve arabica quality, productivity, and climate resilience. It is another sign that big coffee is investing upstream because the future cup starts at farm level.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Next story: Royal Cup Coffee and Tea has completed its acquisition of Farmer Brothers Coffee Company, according to Daily Coffee News on May sixth.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: This is a major commercial coffee deal. Royal Cup, founded in 1896 in Birmingham, is combining with Farmer Brothers, founded in 1912 and long known for direct-store delivery.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: The price was $1.29 per share in cash, with a total payout around $28.3 million when restricted stock units and other awards are included.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: The deal takes Farmer Brothers private and ends decades of public trading. Royal Cup gains brands like Boyd's Coffee, SUM ONE Coffee Roasters, West Coast Coffee, Cain's, and China Mist.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: This is not the tiny single-origin pour-over side of coffee. This is foodservice, hospitality, healthcare, convenience, office coffee, and retail routes. The coffee you meet in conference rooms.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: And those channels matter. They shape everyday coffee expectations for millions of people who may never read a tasting note longer than medium roast.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: It also shows how scale is becoming more attractive as costs rise. Distribution networks, route density, and national accounts can be the difference between margin and migraine.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: Speaking of costs, our third story is the uncomfortable one: the war in Iran is making coffee production more expensive, with fertilizer and energy markets feeling the shock.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Daily Coffee News reported that the International Coffee Organization tied the conflict to a 2.3 percent increase in its composite indicator price, but the bigger concern is the 2026 and 2027 crop cycle.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: The World Bank projected fertilizer prices rising 31 percent in 2026, with urea jumping 60 percent and energy prices rising 24 percent. For farmers, that is not abstract.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Especially because fertilizer is already a big chunk of production cost. In Colombia, for example, it can represent roughly 18 to 20 percent of parchment coffee production costs.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: And Colombia's coffee federation reported imported urea prices moving from $414 to $750 per metric ton. For smallholders, that can mean less fertilizer, lower yields, or thinner household income.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Brazil has its own exposure because a significant share of imported urea came from the Middle East. Costa Rica officials warned about a potential perfect storm for the next harvest.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: The key nuance: the 2025 and 2026 crop may be less affected because fertilizer was already applied in many places. But the following season is where the pain could show up.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: So if your favorite cafe has been carefully explaining why green coffee prices, freight, packaging, rent, and wages are all moving, this is another piece of the puzzle.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: Exactly. Specialty coffee cannot talk about quality without talking about producer economics. A great cup starts with farmers being able to afford the inputs and labor that quality requires.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Fourth story: coffee science gave us a legitimately fascinating mechanism. Texas A and M researchers identified a pathway that may help explain coffee's health benefits.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: The study, covered by Daily Coffee News on May fifth and published in Nutrients, looked at compounds in brewed coffee binding to a receptor called NR4A1.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: NR4A1 is involved in stress response, inflammation, metabolism, and cellular damage. The researchers described it as a kind of nutrient sensor.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: The fun twist is that caffeine was not the star. Polyphenolic compounds like caffeic acid, chlorogenic acid, and ferulic acid appeared more active in the models.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: So decaf drinkers can finally look the espresso crowd in the eye and say, my cup has biochemical dignity.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: Please do not say that to your barista during rush. But yes, it helps explain why large population studies often see benefits with both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: There are caveats, of course. This is mechanistic lab work, not a prescription to replace lunch with a carafe.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: Correct. Coffee is complex, health is complex, and adding whipped cream until the cup has a skyline may alter the wellness narrative.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: Finally, competition corner: Sprudge highlighted free U.S. Barista Championship preparation workshops from U.S. Coffee Championships and Dalla Corte.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: The May ninth workshop is at Onyx Coffee Lab headquarters in Rogers, Arkansas, following an earlier Olympia Coffee session in Washington. An East Coast session is still to be announced.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: The workshops cover rules, sensory exercises, technical evaluations, mock run-throughs, judges' deliberation, and hands-on familiarity with competition equipment.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: I love that because competitions can look glamorous from the outside, but the learning curve is steep. Free community workshops lower the intimidation factor.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: And if you have ever watched someone practice a ten-minute routine forty times, you know barista competition is performance art plus spreadsheet plus controlled panic.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: Beautifully said. Today's through-line is that coffee is getting more professional at every layer: sourcing standards, corporate scale, farm economics, lab science, and competition training.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: The practical takeaway: support roasters doing transparent work, be kind when menu prices move, and maybe give decaf a little respect.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: And if you are heading to a competition workshop today, bring curiosity, a notebook, and maybe a snack. Calibration is easier when your blood sugar is not filing a complaint.

lines.speaker: Milo
lines.text: That's The Daily Grind for Saturday. I'm Milo, wishing your espresso shots run sweet and your grinder retention be tiny.

lines.speaker: Riley
lines.text: And I'm Riley. Brew something beautiful, tip your barista, and we'll catch you tomorrow.
